power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Stress generation describes processes by which individuals actively contribute to the occurrence of self-generated stressful events.
Personal characteristics like neuroticism or psychopathology have been found to predict the occurrence of major life stressors over several months or years.
However, a profound understanding of stress generation over shorter time periods in people's daily lives is still missing.
Here, we integrated recent research on personenvironment transactions from personality psychology into the clinical stress generation literature to develop a process model of stress generation.

This process model posits that stress generation unfolds across multiple timescales and that short-term dynamics between momentary, state-level personal characteristics and daily hassles are the building blocks for established long-term stress generation effects.
To evaluate a core aspect of this model, we conducted a systematic literature search on stress generation in daily life (45 studies, Ntotal = 9'818).
Results show that both dispositional traits and momentary states predict the occurrence of daily hassles, supporting the existence and relevance of stress generation in daily life.
However, future research on stress generation across timescales is needed to test the theorized link between stress generation in daily life and long-term stress generation effects.
Stress is a common and normative experience, but some people face more stressful events than others (Liu & Alloy, 2010; Rnic et al., 2023).

text.text: In this review, we propose a process model that focuses on stress generation in daily life by integrating insights and methods from personality psychology into clinical stress generation literature.

text.text: Stress exposure describes the confrontation with stressful events that exceed personal resources and can elicit a stress response.

In this review, we differentiate between two types of stress exposure, daily hassles and major life stressors, and we use the term stressful events when we refer to both types.

text.text: Thus, stress generation can be more generally defined as processes by which individuals actively contribute to the occurrence of dependent stressful events.

text.text: The lion's share of existing theory and research has focused on long-term stress generation, relying on longitudinal designs with assessments every few months or years to investigate whether and how personal characteristics predict the subsequent occurrence of dependent major life stressors.
In a recent meta-analysis, Rnic et al. (2023) integrated evidence from 95 longitudinal studies on clinical predictors of long-term stress generation.

text.text: Across these studies, a mediumsized link between general psychopathology and the occurrence of dependent stressful events was found (r = .23), suggesting that people with elevated psychopathology experience more dependent stress than people with lower psychopathology levels.
These predictive links seemed to generalize across different types of psychopathology, highlighting that stress generation is not specific to depression (Hammen, 2006; Liu et al., 2024).

text.text: Furthermore, there is evidence that not only clinical disorders and general psychopathology but also broader risk factors, such as maladaptive interpersonal behaviors, can predict the occurrence of dependent major life stressors. Santee et al. (2023) meta-analytically examined different clusters of risk factors that were theorized to predict stress generation.

text.text: Integrating evidence from 70 longitudinal studies, the authors found that (1) maladaptive emotion regulation behaviors, (2) disinhibition and antagonism, (3) avoidance, (4) repetitive negative thinking, (5) negative cognitive content, (6) excessive self-standards, (7) pervasive negative affect, and (8) other-oriented focus predicted the occurrence of dependent stressful events (.10 ≤ r ≤ .26).

For example, pervasive negative affect as captured by the personality trait neuroticism has emerged as a robust predictor of several dependent major life stressors such as unemployment and divorce (E. D. Beck & Jackson, 2022; Santee et al., 2023; Soto, 2019).

text.text: The practical relevance of these stress generation effects is underlined by evidence that major life stressors predict the onset of mental disorders, well-being decreases, and increases in maladaptive personal characteristics (Bühler et al., 2024; Cohen et al., 2019; Hammen, 2005; Kendler et al., 1999).

text.text: Stress generation processes may thus lead to a vicious cycle of maladaptive personal characteristics and stressful events (Hammen, 2006; Liu, 2013).

text.text: Similarly, in their meta-analysis, Rnic et al. (2023) found a significant indirect effect of stressful events on increases in psychopathology ( = .04), indicating that generated stress can exacerbate psychopathology.

text.text: In summary, existing research and meta-analytic reviews provide convincing evidence for the existence and significance of long-term stress generation effects, with different types of psychopathology and psychological risk factors predicting the occurrence of dependent major life stressors over several month or years.

Based on this evidence, initial theoretical models of stress generation have been developed to explain the relationship across different predictors of stress generation and integrate different research lines into a coherent framework (Harkness & Washburn, 2016; Liu, 2013).

text.text: These models converge on a causal chain that links distal risk factors to dependent stressful events through cognitive/personality risk factors and proximal behavioral risk factors.

For example, genetic differences are theorized to be distal risk factors of high levels of neuroticism; high levels of neuroticism, in turn, are proposed to lead to maladaptive behaviors like reassurance seeking, which should cause the occurrence of dependent stressful events.

These theoretical propositions reflect the conceptual origin of the Stress Generation Hypothesis as an action theory (Hammen, 2006), suggesting that people's behaviors are powerful predictors of environmental changes (Liu, 2013).

text.text: However, contemporary theory and research on stress generation share several limitations that inhibit their ability to explain the mechanisms of stress generation and spark the development of effective interventions.
First, existing theoretical accounts remain relatively vague regarding the timescale on which stress generation unfolds (Starr et al., 2025).
text.formatted: First, existing theoretical accounts remain relatively vague regarding the timescale on which stress generation unfolds <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">(Starr et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: That is, it remains unclear whether stress generation predictors, such as personality pathology or reassurance seeking, are theorized to predict the occurrence of dependent stressful events over hours, days, weeks, or years.

This limitation is not specific to stress generation theory but is a common problem across psychological theories, providing little guidance for design choices in longitudinal research (Haehner, Driver, et al., 2025; Hopwood, Bleidorn, et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This limitation is not specific to stress generation theory but is a common problem across psychological theories, providing little guidance for design choices in longitudinal research <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Haehner, Driver, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Hopwood, Bleidorn, et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: So far, stress generation has mostly been examined over months and years, which likely has to do with the typical length of assessment waves in longitudinal designs in psychological science.
For example, the average time lag between assessments in the meta-analyses by Rnic et al. (2023) and Santee et al. (2023) were 21 months or 16 months, respectively.
text.formatted: For example, the average time lag between assessments in the meta-analyses by <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">Rnic et al. (2023)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">Santee et al. (2023)</ref> were 21 months or 16 months, respectively.

text.text: As a result, we still have a limited understanding of whether and how stress generation processes unfold over shorter time periods of several hours or days.
Second, existing stress generation theories describe the predictors and outcomes of stress generation in a broad way.
For instance, Liu (2013) posited that behavioral risk factors like excessive reassurance seeking predict the occurrence of dependent stressful events.
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Liu (2013)</ref> posited that behavioral risk factors like excessive reassurance seeking predict the occurrence of dependent stressful events.

text.text: However, this description leaves it unclear whether reassurance seeking predicts the occurrence of daily hassles or major life stressor and whether research should assess reassurance seeking in a given moment or a person's general tendency to seek reassurance.
Thus, contemporary stress generation theories may be not specific enough to derive testable hypotheses about stress generation.

Third, existing research has focused primarily on between-person differences in stress generation, linking individual differences in depressive symptoms, neuroticism, or personality pathology to the occurrence of dependent stressful events (Allen et al., 2022; Elliot et al., 2011; Flynn & Rudolph, 2011; Goldstein et al., 2021; Hasegawa et al., 2023).

text.text: This perspective matches the original proposition of the Stress Generation Hypothesis, which states that people with depressive symptomatology tend to experience more dependent stressors than those without (Hammen, 1991).

text.text: However, within-person analyses examining how momentary thoughts, feelings, and behaviors predict the occurrence of stressful events for a specific individual are needed to complement this between-person approach (Modersitzki et al., 2025; Phan et al., 2025).

text.text: Investigating how stress generation unfolds within individuals may also guide the development of effective interventions aimed at disrupting stress generation.
To overcome these limitations, we suggest integrating the clinical literature on stress generation with theory and research on person-environment transactions from personality science.
Person-environment transactions capture the various ways in which personal and environmental variables relate to each other over time (Rauthmann, 2021).
text.formatted: Person-environment transactions capture the various ways in which personal and environmental variables relate to each other over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">(Rauthmann, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Stress generation can be conceptualized as a specific type of person-environment transactions.
Theory and research on stress generation may thus benefit from integrating recent advancement in the description of person-environment transactions.

The study of person-environment transactions has a long tradition in personality science -ranging from early research on person-situation interactions (Allport, 1961; Lewin, 1936) to recent examinations of event-related personality change (Bleidorn et al., 2020; Bühler et al., 2024).

text.text: Thus, integrating personality science into stress generation research is a way to advance both fields by merging theories and aggregating research findings.

One of the most important theoretical advancements in personality science has been the adoption of a process perspective, connecting momentary person-environment dynamics to long-term transactions between individuals and their environment (Baumert et al., 2017; Bleidorn et al., 2020).

text.text: Prominent examples of this perspective include the Whole Trait Theory (Fleeson & Jayawickreme, 2015), the TESSERA Framework (Wrzus & Roberts, 2017), the Integrative-State-Trait Process Model (Geukes et al., 2018), and the Person-Environment Relations Model (Rauthmann, 2021).

text.text: These theories have three key aspects in common.
First, they distinguish between state-and trait-level personal characteristics.

Trait-level characteristics describe people's stable patterns of thoughts, feelings, and behaviors across situations, whereas states capture momentary thoughts, feelings, and behavior in a given situation (Allemand & Flückiger, 2017; A. J. Wright et al., 2026; Wrzus & Roberts, 2017).

text.text: For example, neuroticism is typically assessed as a stable trait capturing people's general tendency to perceive the world as threatening place, experience negative affect, and worry in stressful situations (Goldberg, 1992; Soto & John, 2017), whereas state neuroticism captures instances of negative affect or rumination in a given moment.

text.text: For example, the Integrative-State-Trait Process Model (Geukes et al., 2018) posits that a person selects a behavior based on social cues in the environment and mental processing of these cues, which may become a habit over time and elicit environmental changes.

text.text: This model emphasizes the dynamic interactions between people and their environment at an individual level and may be helpful for the development of effective intervention approaches.

Third, another common theme across different process theories of person-environment transactions is the causal relevance of momentary dynamics for long-term longitudinal developments (Bleidorn et al., 2020; Geukes et al., 2018; Wrzus & Roberts, 2017).

text.text: For example, the TESSERA Framework (Wrzus & Roberts, 2017) suggests that momentary dynamics across situations, states, and reactions are the building blocks for long-term personality trait changes.

text.text: According to this model, enduring changes in the characteristics of everyday situations and in momentary personality state expressions may accumulate over time to manifest as long-term personality development.

Integrating these ideas about person-environment transactions into stress generation research may offer new perspectives on this type of transaction and guide future research on stress generation across timescales.

text.text: The next part of the causal chain -trait-level personal characteristics -are likely the most researched predictors of stress generation.

Drawing on evidence from recent meta-analytic reviews, it can be expected that (1) psychopathology, (2) maladaptive emotion regulation, (3) disinhibition and antagonism, (4) avoidance, (5) repetitive negative thinking, (6) pervasive negative affect, (7) negative cognitive styles, (8) other-oriented focus, and (9) excessive selfstandards are trait characteristics that prospectively predict the occurrence of dependent stressful events (Rnic et al., 2023; Santee et al., 2023).

text.text: However, in contrast to existing stress generation theories, the current process model posits that these trait-level characteristics do not directly predict the occurrence of dependent stressors but that these effects are mediated by short-term dynamics that unfold in people's daily lives.
In other words, we hypothesize that links between momentary, state-level characteristics and daily hassles are the building blocks of long-term stress generation effects.

For example, people with higher levels of trait neuroticism may be more likely to experience a divorce because of the accumulation of relationship conflicts triggered by momentary neurotic behaviors in daily life.

At the core of the process model are state-level personal characteristics, which depend on a person's traits and the characteristics of the situation (Fleeson & Jayawickreme, 2015; Rauthmann et al., 2015; Sherman et al., 2015; Wrzus & Roberts, 2017).

A Process Model of Stress Generation Note.
Genes and childhood maltreatment are distal risk factors of stress generation as they increase the likelihood of maladaptive traits.
Maladaptive traits (e.g., psychopathology) serve as predictors of dependent daily hassles and dependent major life stressors.
However, these links are theorized to be mediated via short-term dynamics that occur in people's daily lives over several minutes or hours.
State characteristics comprising momentary thoughts, feelings, and behaviors depend on a person's trait and the characteristics of the situation.
Behavioral states then cause the occurrence of dependent hassles.
Daily hassles accumulate over time to cause dependent major life stressors.
However, in rare cases, momentary behaviors may also directly cause the occurrence of dependent major life stressors.

We describe the links between trait characteristics, state characteristics, and dependent daily hassles as stress generation in daily life because they focus on short-term outcomes of stress generation processes.  b This hypothesis reflects the conceptual origin of stress generation theory as an action theory (Hammen, 2006).

text.text: However, to the best of our knowledge, convincing tests that specific behaviors are causally linked to the occurrence of dependent stressful events is still missing.
Stress generation in daily life can be defined as links between trait-level characteristics, state-level characteristics, and the occurrence of dependent daily hassles.

Similar to major life stressors, daily hassles have been found to predict lasting well-being decreases and the onset of mental disorders (Asselmann et al., 2017; Chan et al., 2016; Haehner et al., 2024; Mroczek & Almeida, 2004; Zheng et al., 2023), underlining the practical relevance of examining stress generation in daily life.

text.text: Stress generation in daily life can be investigated with intensive longitudinal designs such as experience sampling and daily-diary research.

With these designs, participants typically rate their trait-level characteristics at baseline and report state-level characteristics and the occurrence of daily hassles once per day or multiple times per day (Eberhart & Hammen, 2009; Mandel et al., 2018; Vize et al., 2024).

text.text: To overcome these problems, we conducted a systematic review that summarizes and integrates existing research on stress generation in daily life.
The systematic review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement (Page et al., 2021).

We conducted a systematic literature search using PsycINFO on October 9, 2024 and updated the literature search on February 27, 2026 with the following search string: ("stress generation" OR "generation of stress*" OR "generated stress*" OR "dependent stress*" OR "life event*" OR "stressful event*" OR "minor event*" OR "daily stressor*" OR "hassle*" OR "daily stress*") AND ("daily diary" OR "daily-diary" OR "ESM" OR "experience sampling"
OR "momentary assessment" OR "ambulatory assessment" OR "daily life" OR "diary").
Search results were restricted to studies written in English and published from 1991 onward (i.e., the year when the Stress Generation Hypothesis was introduced).
This database literature search resulted in 1,488 studies that were then screened for eligibility.
Furthermore, we conducted a backward search by screening the reference list of existing review articles on stress generation (Liu et al., 2024; Rnic et al., 2023; Santee et al., 2023).

text.text: Studies that fulfilled the following criteria were included in the systematic review: (1) empirical, quantitative study with human subjects, (2) written in English, (3) experience sampling or daily-diary design, (4) assessment of stressor occurrence 2 (i.e., stress assessment did not confound subjective stress perception and stress exposure), (5) no intervention, and (6) examination of stress generation processes in daily life.
The latter was defined as studies that examined a predictive link between a personal characteristic and the occurrence of daily hassles.

Divergent codings were resolved through discussion.

To facilitate knowledge integration, we meta-analytically aggregated available effect size information if standardized effect size measures (i.e., correlations or odds ratios) on personstressor links were provided in at least three independent studies.
To do so, we first transformed all effect size measures to correlations and then transformed all correlations to z values using Fisher's r-to-z transformation.
Second, we aggregated these effect sizes using multi-level random effect meta-analysis with effect sizes nested in studies as implemented in the metafor package (Viechtbauer, 2010).

text.text: Overall, 45 studies with 44 unique samples and 161 unique person-stressors links were included in this review.
The included studies were published between 1991 and 2025 (M = 2014.84, SD = 8.40), with 93% (k = 42) being published journal articles and 7% (k = 3) being PhD theses.
On average, intensive longitudinal data collections lasted for 14.02 days (SD = 10.34) with 2.71 (SD = 3.04) assessments per day.
Sample sizes ranged from 60 to 2'016 participants, with an average sample size of N = 223.14 (SD = 303.31).
Samples were mostly college samples (k = 18, 41%) or convenience samples (k = 17, 39%), relatively young (M = 33.47, SD = 14.23), and primarily female (M = 68%, SD = 19.41).
Furthermore, samples were almost exclusively recruited in the US (k = 32, 97%).
Daily hassles were mostly assessed using checklist methods (k = 113, 70%), with only 23% of measures (k = 37) distinguishing between dependent and independent hassles.
On average, hassles were assessed 2.25 times per day (SD = 2.78), whereas personal characteristics were assessed less than once per day (M = 0.59, SD = 0.94).

Furthermore, personal characteristics were primarily assessed using self-reports (k = 132, 82%), with sleep behavior (k = 31), negative affect (k = 18), and neuroticism (k = 13) being assessed most frequently.

Complicating knowledge aggregation, only 40% of person-stressor links were quantified using standardized effect sizes such as correlations (k = 42) or Odds Ratios (k = 23), whereas most person-stressor links were only reported as unstandardized coefficients in multilevel models (k = 76, 47%).
Finally, of the 161 unique links on stress generation in daily life, 93 examined traitlevel predictors of daily hassles and 68 examined state-level predictors.

The examination of trait-level predictors of daily hassles allows insights into whether variables that have been found to predict stress generation in the long run can also predict stressful events over shorter time periods.

text.text: In the following, we summarize findings for trait-level characteristics that were examined in at least three independent studies, with meta-analytic estimates being provided if standardized effect size estimates from at least three independent studies were available (i.e., neuroticism and depression).
Neuroticism.
Neuroticism was the most frequently examined predictor of daily hassles (12 studies).
Overall, there was consistent evidence that higher levels of neuroticism predict stress generation in daily life.
This conclusion was also supported by the meta-analytic aggregation of standardized effect size estimates (see Figure 3A).
text.formatted: This conclusion was also supported by the meta-analytic aggregation of standardized effect size estimates (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3A</ref>).

text.text: Higher levels of neuroticism showed a small positive relationship with the occurrence of daily hassles, r = .10, p = .039, 95% CI = [.01, .18].

However, effect sizes varied substantially across studies (I² = 60%) and none of the included studies had examined the hypothesis that neuroticism predicts the occurrence of dependent but not independent daily hassles.

In line with the initial proposition of the Stress Generation Hypothesis (Hammen, 1991), higher levels of depressive symptoms or the diagnosis of a depressive disorder predicted the occurrence of daily hassles (9 studies).

Extraversion was examined as predictor of the occurrence of daily hassles in four intensive longitudinal studies.
In line with meta-analytic research on long-term stress generation (Santee et al., 2023), these studies converge on the finding that extraversion is not a significant predictor of daily hassles.

This initial research showed that higher levels of personality pathology predict more frequent occurrences of daily hassles.

Three intensive longitudinal studies investigated trait negative affect as predictor of daily hassles.

Two of these studies found that trait negative affect did not predict the occurrence of dependent daily hassles (Kelso, 2023; Shih & Auerbach, 2010), whereas Veilleux et al. (2020) found that a more negative affect balance predicted a higher number of daily hassles.

Sleep was examined most frequently as state-level predictor of the occurrence of daily hassles (7 studies).
However, evidence on whether worse sleep predicts stress generation in daily life was mixed.

text.text: In sum, although there is tentative evidence that worse sleep predicts the occurrence of daily hassles, future research is warranted to clarify under which circumstances sleep may or may not predict the occurrence of (dependent) daily hassles.
Six studies considered momentary negative affect as state-level predictor of stress generation in daily life.
The available research suggests that the link between negative affect and daily hassles depends on the time lag between assessments.

That is, while most studies found that higher levels of negative affect predicted the occurrence of daily hassles at the same assessment (Haliczer et al., 2021; Kiang & Buchanan, 2014), negative affect did not predict subsequent hassle occurrences (Sahl et al., 2009; Vize et al., 2024).

text.text: Thus, negative affect seems to be a state-level predictor of daily hassles, but the temporal unfolding of this link requires further research.

text.text: However, more research on the links between momentary personal characteristics and the occurrence of daily hassles is needed to evaluate the replicability of these effects.

Integrating ideas from personality psychology into clinical psychology, we proposed a process model of stress generation that provides a roadmap for future research on stress generation across timescales.

This process model posits that dynamics between state-level characteristics and daily hassles accumulate over time and explain well-established long-term longitudinal links between trait characteristics and major life stressors.
We aimed to evaluate a core aspect of this model -stress generation effects in daily life -in a systematic review.
This review showed that trait-characteristics like depression and neuroticism predict the occurrence of daily hassles (r = .10 to .11).
In contrast, evidence was less clear regarding the predictive effects of momentary characteristics -particularly momentary behaviors -on stress generation in daily life.
We found tentative evidence for negative affect and sleep problems as state-level predictors of daily hassles.
However, future research is needed to test which momentary thoughts, feelings, and behaviors predict the occurrence of daily hassles within individuals.
Furthermore, the theorized link between stress generation in daily life and long-term stress generation has yet to be tested.
The systematic literature review revealed that empirical evidence for stress generation in daily life is still limited.
There are at least five important directions for future research.

First, more intensive longitudinal research is needed to evaluate the replicability of person-stressor links in daily life and to examine a broader set of personal characteristics as predictors of daily hassles.

Compared to the rich empirical literature on long-term stress generation processes, studies examining stress generation in daily life have only recently taken root in psychology (Liu et al., 2024; Rnic et al., 2023; Santee et al., 2023).

text.text: However, with technological advancements, the required intensive longitudinal data collections on stress generation in daily life became more manageable, allowing researchers to examine the links between state-level personal characteristics and daily hassles in relatively large samples.
Future research should continue these efforts and examine a broad set of (state-level) personal characteristics as predictors of daily hassles at a time.
Such research would also allow us to investigate the unique contribution of each characteristic and to test whether behavioral states are indeed the most potent predictor of daily hassles.

Furthermore, multi-method approaches are warranted that combine self-reports, other-reports, and mobile sensing to better capture momentary behaviors as active ingredients of stress generation in daily life.
Second, a more thorough investigation of daily hassles as outcomes of stress generation processes is needed.
Stress generation theory posits that personal characteristics predict the occurrence of dependent but not independent stressors (Hammen, 1991; Liu, 2013).

text.text: In longterm longitudinal studies, life event interviews are typically used to distinguish between dependent and independent major life stressors and to disentangle stressor occurrence and stressor perception (Dohrenwend, 2006; Hammen, 2006; Liu et al., 2024).

text.text: However, such interview approaches can be too burdensome for intensive longitudinal data collections and frequently occurring daily hassles (Starr et al., 2025; but see Almeida et al., 2002).

text.text: As a result, most studies included in the systematic review have not distinguished between dependent and independent hassles, providing only a partial test of stress generation theory.
Technological advancements like the rise of large-language models may help to overcome this problem.
That is, participants could describe daily hassles in an open-response format and large-language models could then be trained to categorize these descriptions as dependent or independent.

Critically, to minimize confounding between personal characteristics and the likelihood of reporting events as hassles, it may be advisable to ask participants to describe all significant event occurrences-not only negative ones-and subsequently have raters or large language models code whether each event is objectively stressful based on the provided free-text descriptions.

Furthermore, checklist approaches, though often criticized in long-term stress generation research, may be well suited for intensive longitudinal designs, because the frequent assessments can help mitigate memory biases (Starr et al., 2025).

text.text: Finally, the assessment of daily hassles may be enriched by new information sources, such as mobile sensing, to assess relevant characteristics of daily hassles (e.g., location) holistically and objectively (Harari et al., 2021; Mehl, 2024).

text.text: Third, the stress generation process model predicts that short-term dynamics between state-level personal characteristics and daily hassles contribute to long-term stress generation effects.

However, direct evidence for this link of stress generation processes across timescales is still scarce. Eberhart and Hammen (2009) combined a 1-month longitudinal design and a 2- week daily-diary study in the same sample to show that trait-and state-level characteristics (e.g., anxious attachment) predicted the occurrence of interpersonal stressors across different timescales.

text.text: However, this study did not test the core hypothesis that accumulation of short-term effects mediated the long-term links between trait-level characteristics and interpersonal stressful events.
A first study that has examined the relationship between stress generation in daily life and long-term stress generation found relatively small and inconsistent associations (Haehner et al., 2026).

text.text: Clarifying the unfolding of stress generation across timescales likely is a challenging endeavor, because effects may differ across people and across time intervals.

One important direction for future research would be systematically vary the number of assessments and time intervals between assessments to better characterize the timescale of stress generation processes.
Such a systematic examination with varying time intervals between assessments would be critical to determine the temporal unfolding of stress generation (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: Such a systematic examination with varying time intervals between assessments would be critical to determine the temporal unfolding of stress generation (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>).

text.text: Once research on the timescale of stress generation processes becomes available, a formalized theoretical model of stress generation including precise mathematical predictions on the links between personal characteristics and the occurrence of stressful events can be developed.
Fourth, the stress generation process model posits causal relationships across personal characteristics, dependent daily hassles, and major life stressors.
In this systematic review, we focused on intensive longitudinal data collections that examined whether personal characteristics predicted the occurrence of daily hassles over time.

The longitudinal perspective enabled a closer approximation to causal inference, because lagged effects of state-level personal characteristics at time point t on the occurrence of hassles at time point t + 1 establish a clearer temporal ordering of effects (Starr et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The longitudinal perspective enabled a closer approximation to causal inference, because lagged effects of state-level personal characteristics at time point t on the occurrence of hassles at time point t + 1 establish a clearer temporal ordering of effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">(Starr et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, longitudinal designs and the examination of lagged effects alone are not sufficient to prove causality.

To strengthen causal inferences in observational data, researchers should specify hypotheses and assumptions regarding the underlying causal net of variables involved in the stress generation process using, for example, directed analytic graphs (Grosz et al., 2020; Rohrer, 2018).

text.text: Furthermore, experimental approaches need to be incorporated into stress generation research more regularly.
So far, research on interventions aimed to prevent or disrupt stress generation is fairly limited (but see Jones et al., 2023).
text.formatted: So far, research on interventions aimed to prevent or disrupt stress generation is fairly limited (but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Jones et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, such research would be theoretically and practically relevant as it could help to examine the causal relevance of specific predictors of stress generation.
Furthermore, if successful, such interventions could be applied in psychotherapeutic settings to disrupt vicious cycles between maladaptive personal characteristics and stressful events.
Fifth, research on stress generation in daily life is currently limited by the fact that evidence stems almost exclusively from the United States.
Furthermore, samples included in the systematic review were primarily female and relatively young (Harrison et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Furthermore, samples included in the systematic review were primarily female and relatively young <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Harrison et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, stress generation research using culturally diverse, gender-balanced, and age-heterogenous samples is warranted to better understand the cross-cultural generalizability and replicability of stress generation in daily life across different samples.
Although future research on the stress generation process model is needed, it may already inform the development of interventions to reduce or avoid stress generation.
As can be seen in Figure 1, stress generation interventions could intervene at different points of the causal chain to disrupt stress generation processes.

text.text: One strategy -consistent with this process model and other stress generation theories (Liu, 2013; Liu et al., 2024) -would be to change maladaptive trait levels to prevent stress generation.

text.text: For example, reducing people's enduring patterns of negative affect or negative cognitive styles would decrease the likelihood of maladaptive momentary feelings or thoughts, and, as a result, disrupt both short-and long-term stress generation processes.

According to the stress generation process model, another intervention strategy would be to disrupt stress generation in daily life by reducing maladaptive states or by disrupting the link between maladaptive momentary behaviors and daily hassles.

For example, offering support when people are in a vulnerable state with high levels of negative affect could reduce negative affect in this moment, decrease the likelihood of maladaptive behaviors, and thus disrupt short-and long-term stress generation processes (Everitt et al., 2021; Haehner, Wright, et al., 2025) Second, research on stress generation in daily life is still in its infancy.

Future research on stress generation in daily life is needed to test, for instance, moderating effects of different assessment methods, different study designs, or different assessment intervals.

This process model thus proposes a new perspective on stress generation by integrating momentary stress generation dynamics that unfold over several minutes or hours into existing theory and research about long-term stress generation processes.
As some parts of the model are still speculative, it can be understood as a proposal for future research on stress generation across timescales.
Specifically, core aspects of the model, referring to stress generation in daily life and the link between short-and long-term stress generation, have received relatively little empirical attention.
For instance, integrative research efforts that summarize evidence on the links between trait-level characteristics, state-level characteristics, and dependent daily hassles are missing.

As such, the proposed process model provides a starting point for the development of a just-in-time adaptive intervention against stress generation.
Just-in-time adaptive interventions seek to provide the right amount of support at the right time to increase intervention effectiveness (Nahum-Shani et al., 2015).

The development of such just-in-time adaptive interventions requires insights into the processes that mediate distal intervention outcomes to identify intervention points and tailoring options (Nahum-Shani et al., 2018).
The stress generation process model provides these insights by connecting short-and long-term stress generation processes.LimitationsThe present review has several limitations.

First, the non-representativeness of stress generation research in terms of the global population limits the generalizability of existing findings about stress generation, including the conclusions presented in this review.
While we assume stress generation to be a culturally-universal phenomenon, the specific person-stressor links likely differ across cultures, outlining an important direction for future research.

Although the understanding of stress generation has increased substantially over the last decades, the unfolding of stress generation processes in people's daily lives has received little attention so far, limiting our ability to understand stress generation processes within individuals and develop effective interventions against it.To overcome these limitations, we developed a process model of stress generation that integrates research from personality psychology into clinical stress generation research.
This model posits that short-term stress generation dynamics between state-level personal characteristics and dependent daily hassles are the building blocks of long-term stress generation effects.

In a systematic review, we showed that trait characteristics, like depression and neuroticism, and state-level characteristics, like momentary negative affect, predicted the occurrence of daily hassles, supporting core aspects of the stress generation process model.
